events.name: The World & Me: Pulse with Company E and Sound Impact
events.description: Join us for a special The World & Me as we celebrate unique movement and patterns on the planet we call home with local dancers from Company | E , musicians from Sound Impact , and educators from the National Museum of Natural History. Watch a performance titled PULSE* and stay afterwards to explore different hands-on activities with museum specimens. Performance will be 10:30 - 11:20. Hands-on stations and activities will be open 11:30 - 12:30. More about Pulse Everything, including the Earth, has its own unique pulse, and those pulses form the heartbeat of the Earth and of us all. COMPANY E’s PULSE is a 45 minute performance created by storytellers, choreographers, dancers, musicians and scientists.Told with humour and empathy, the show deploys dance, live and recorded music, storytelling, and student engagement to embrace the power, the joy and the magic of the Earth and all its inhabitants. It’s all told through one character’s search for his own heartbeat, his own pulse, in place of his preoccupation with his technology. It’s a STEAM-based journey through time and space discovering in every living thing, including the planet itself, a PULSE, and that ultimately our impulse to protect it in the end serves as well to protect us. About Company | E Company | E is a DC-based repertory dance company whose work is created through international artistic and cultural exchanges. Using dance, music, storytelling, filmmaking and the Metaverse, the Company uses art to bridge cultural divides, speak to the critical issues of our time and honor the idea that “there is more than unites us than divides us,” Company | E serves as Cultural Diplomats with the U.S. Department of State, and educators of artists of all ages around the globe. The Company embraces the overarching “E” words that it was named for: ecology, equity, excitement, energy, education, engagement, and so many more. Q?rius is located on the right as you enter the museum. events.name: Where Home Takes Flight: Painting Mini-Birdhouses
events.description: Celebrate creativity, family, and the idea of “home” in this hands-on mini-birdhouse painting workshop designed for all ages. Inspired by the beauty of nature and the meaning of safe spaces, participants will decorate their own wooden mini-birdhouses using vibrant paints, patterns, and personal touches. Families are invited to work together to design birdhouses that reflect their unique stories, cultures, and creativity. Whether you choose bold colors, meaningful symbols, or playful designs, each piece becomes a one-of-a-kind expression of what “home” means to you—and a welcoming space for our feathered neighbors. All materials will be provided, including birdhouses, paints, brushes, and decorative elements. No prior experience is necessary—just bring your imagination! events.name: Feed Me Now and Evermore: The Enduring Power of African American Sunday Suppers
events.description: Rhythms, Roots, Recipes: Community Stories of Food and Music brings together cooking demonstrations, live music, and storytelling. Each program in the series explores traditions that animate families and communities across the United States—and beyond. In many African American homes, the Sunday supper remains an important moment to reconnect among family, honor ancestral ties, and share recipes reflecting history, faith, and community. In this cooking demonstration, chef and artist Roscoe Hall and author and food historian Adrian Miller explore why the Sunday supper continues to be a cornerstone of family and cultural life. As Hall prepares brown butter crab rice and gumbo, Arkansas-based S. Juain Young and Artists United perform songs from the African American church that have long nourished hearts, souls, and movements.

events.name: Kronos Quartet
events.description: As part of our commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the National Museum of American History invites visitors to join us in the Warner Bros. Theater as the internationally acclaimed Kronos Quartet presents an afternoon of music spanning cultures and generations, exploring themes of resilience, loss, preservation, and remembrance. At the center of the program is Steve Reich’s WTC 9/11 , a work that weaves together live performance with recorded voices from NORAD communications, FDNY radio transmissions, and interviews with people who lived and worked in lower Manhattan. The program includes works by Terry Riley, Neil Young, Laurie Anderson, Trevor Weston, and Aftab Darvishi, among others. Kronos will also perform Stacy Garrop’s Glorious Mahalia , a work recently released on the Smithsonian Folkways label that utilizes recordings of civil rights visionary Mahalia Jackson. Following the performance, members of the Kronos Quartet will join museum staff for a conversation about the music and its themes. ------------ Full Program: John Oswald / Excerpt from Spectre * Terry Riley / One Earth, One People, One Love from Sun Rings * Neil Young (arr. events.name: Play Date at NMNH: Megalodon Day!
events.description: Join us Tuesday, September 15th, for a belated celebration of Megalodon Day (June 15th)! While Megalodons, an ancient shark that lived 23 – 3.5 million years ago, are no longer swimming in our ocean, people of all ages are fascinated by its size and large teeth! events.name: History Film Forum presents Faith on Film: American Muslims
events.description: The History Film Forum presents two episodes from the 2026 PBS documentary series “American Muslims: A History Revealed.” The 2026 PBS documentary series “American Muslims: A History Revealed” is six short documentary films that explores the early history of Muslims in America. The series is hosted by three American Muslim journalists: Malika Bilal, Aymann Ismail and Asma Khalid who traveled the country to piece together stories spanning over 200 years. The two episodes, “A Portrait of Freedom” and “Islam at the Nation’s Founding,” will be shown in a special edited version as part of an exploration of Muslim American history in the early United States. A panel discussion will follow the screening. This program is presented in partnership with the museum’s Center for the Understanding of Religion in American History, which explores the influence of religion on every facet of life in the United States. “Faith on Film” is in an ongoing series exploring belief on screen, from the golden age of cinema to binge-worthy shows of the streaming era. Through classics like “The Ten Commandments” and “Yentl” and recent fan favorites including “The Chosen” and “Never Have I Ever,” Hollywood's view of religion has long shaped American culture. The National Museum of American History welcomes visitors of all ages and abilities. This event is wheelchair accessible. Captioning and assistive listening devices will be provided. Additional accommodations are available upon request; please email nmahprograms@si.edu . Two weeks’ notice is preferred. Seating is limited and reservations are recommended. events.description: Join us on Tuesdays for special family play dates with museum educators! This Tuesday will be all about taking a closer look at what life is like in the deep sea at the bottom of the ocean! Even though it is very dark (except for the bioluminescent animals), the deepest parts of the ocean are still full of life. Together we will learn about some of the unique animals that have adapted to live in the deep sea, make artwork inspired by the deep sea, and have the chance to see specimens that once lived at the bottom of the ocean! events.name: Nature Journaling
events.description: Drop by the Enid A. Haupt Garden between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. and join Smithsonian Gardens for nature journaling! Nature journaling is an opportunity for visitors to slow down, reflect, and connect to the gardens. This program is designed to foster appreciation and connection to the natural world through observation, reflection, and creativity. Smithsonian Gardens will provide journals, prompts, and art materials to get you started. All ages are welcome! Find us on the East Terrace of the Haupt Garden, close to the Arts and Industries Building. Recommended metro station: L'Enfant Plaza (Blue, Silver, Orange, Green, and Yellow lines) or Smithsonian (Blue, Silver and Orange lines). And be sure to check out the new Growing Tomorrow exhibition and discover how gardens connect people and plants! Activities may be subject to cancellation or modification due to weather conditions. Please check the Smithsonian Gardens online calendar for the latest information: https://gardens.si.edu/plan-your-visit/events/ This program received support from Smithsonian’s Our Shared Future: 250, a Smithsonian-wide initiative commemorating the nation’s 250th. events.name: The Meaning of Home: A Treasures Zine Project
events.venue: African American History and Culture Museum
events.description: For Ages: 8 and Up What does home mean to you? Is it a place, a person, a favorite object, a family tradition, or a memory you carry with you? Drop in for a hands-on zine-making experience that invites you to explore what home and belonging mean to you. Using photographs, drawings, words, collage, and other creative materials, create a one-of-a-kind zine inspired by the people, places, objects, traditions, and memories you treasure. Bring up to 3 printed personal photos to incorporate into your artwork. All other materials are provided. Reflect on the stories that shape who you are, share ideas with others, and leave with a personal keepsake that captures what “home” means to you. No previous art or zine-making experience is needed.

events.description: Beech Tree Puppets features meaningful stories, artfully told with hand-crafted puppets and sets and the use of simple instruments and beautiful singing. Beech Tree Puppets has performed hundreds of shows in schools, libraries and public spaces all over the greater DC region, including The National Theater in DC, the Atlas Performing Arts Center, and at the Durant Arts Center in Alexandria with the National Puppetry Guild. Ingrid and Ole Hass infuse Beech Tree Puppets with their professional experience in the performing and visual arts. Both hold Masters Degrees in Opera Performance from the North Carolina School of the Arts. Ole also holds a Doctor of Musical Arts Degree from UMD in College Park and Ingrid earned a BA in Studio Art from Smith College. events.name: Educator Workshop: Youth Civic Voice through Stamp Design
events.description: How can tiny postage stamps shape national narratives and amplify civic expression? In this hands‑on session from the National Postal Museum, participants will explore how stamps serve as primary sources that reflect and influence democratic values, U.S. identity, and civic engagement. Centering objects from the museum collection, we’ll examine stamp history, elements of design, and how stamps can elevate youth civic engagement. Participants will then create a stamp‑inspired print using simple, classroom‑ready printmaking techniques. This session blends visual arts, history, and civic learning through close‑looking strategies and hands-on learning that support the expression of civic voice through stamp design. This session is in collaboration with WISIT Institute, DC Project Zero.

events.name: Art Guardians | Family Workshop: Chasing Rainbows
events.description: Why do some objects sparkle with rainbow colors? In this interactive workshop for children ages 6–11 and their caregivers, families investigate the science behind iridescence and discover how art conservators care for shimmering art. First, explore ceramics in A Museum in the Making — some with intentionally created iridescent surfaces and others with rainbow-like sheens that developed over hundreds of years. Then make your own art using materials that change appearance as they catch the light. National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution, Photo by Department of Conservation and Scientific Research

events.name: Broad Stripes and Bright Stars
events.description: Meet Mary Pickersgill, seamstress of the enormous garrison flag that inspired the lyrics to America’s national anthem and later became known as the Star-Spangled Banner. What was it like to live in a nation defending its sovereignty? Learn about the War of 1812, considered America’s Second War of Independence, and about ways that widows like Mary expressed patriotism and resourcefulness through acquired skills and family connections.

events.name: Community Day
events.description: Celebrate Community Day at the National Museum of African Art with a full day of programming! Each September, the museum opens its doors to visitors of all ages to inspire them to learn more about the peoples and cultures of Africa and its diaspora through exhibitions, art-making, live performances, tours, and more! Join us for a Pan African Fabric & Fashon showcase. Designers from nine nations each interpret a shared textile framework that incorporates symbolic references representing the five regions of the African continent— North, East, South, West and Central Africa and highlight the significance of African textile tradition. A Sounds of Africa concert will close the day with Live Arts performances!

Welcome Home: 10 th Anniversary Community Weekend at the Museum is part of the larger celebration, The Reunion. Throughout the weekend, you can experience the joy, creativity, and connections that make the Museum a place for everyone to come together, reflect, and celebrate. THROUGHOUT THE WEEKEND Special 10 th Anniversary Menu Experience Sweet Home Café Celebrate the Museum’s milestone through food and flavor with a special 10th Anniversary menu experience at Sweet Home Café. 10 th Anniversary Merchandise Museum Store Commemorate the Museum’s first decade with special 10 th Anniversary merchandise available in the Museum Store throughout the weekend. events.name: The Seoul Guardians
events.description: Joie Chen, an Emmy-winning anchor and correspondent formerly of CNN, Al Jazeera, and CBS News will join directors Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan, and Cho Chul-young for an onstage conversation after the screening. Watch the Trailer On the night of December 3, 2024, then-president Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law in Korea. He banned all political activities and public assemblies and sent troops to the National Assembly building to seize control. The Seoul Guardians plunges you into the political chaos of that night, with codirecting by three journalists who were there. Lawmakers rush to pass a bill ending martial law as ordinary citizens band together to hold off the soldiers sent to take the building. The winner of multiple film festival awards, this stirring documentary resonates with audiences around the world with its message that democracy is fragile and must be defended. Directors: Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan, and Cho Chul-young. Country: Korea. Released: 2026. Length: 70 min. Format: DCP. Language: Korean with English subtitles. Image courtesy of Asian Shadows

And be sure to check out the nearby Growing Tomorrow garden exhibition about food for the future. Location: Find us in the Food Garden on the east side of the National Museum of American History, near 12 th Street, NW. Parents and guardians must remain with their children. Please come prepared for an outdoor experience. Wildlife and insects, including bees and mosquitoes, are a part of our gardens. Participants are encouraged to bring water, sun protection, their own snacks, and are welcome to bring their own blankets for story time. Activities may be subject to cancellation or modification due to weather conditions. (A little rain won’t keep us away, but we will cancel in case of a heavy downpour or thunderstorm!) Please check the Smithsonian Gardens online calendar for the latest information: https://gardens.si.edu/plan-your-visit/events/ This program received support from Smithsonian’s Our Shared Future: 250, a Smithsonian-wide initiative commemorating the nation’s 250th.
